html:
The calendar of 365 days, with an extra day every fourth year, that Julius Caesar brought in from 1 January 45 BCE.

The old Roman year had 355 days. Priests were meant to add an extra month now and then to keep it in line with the seasons, but they did so to suit politics, and by Caesar's time the calendar was about three months out. As chief priest, pontifex maximus, Caesar fixed it with advice from the Alexandrian astronomer Sosigenes. The year 46 BCE was stretched to 445 days to catch up, and from then on the year followed the sun, much as the Egyptian calendar of Ptolemaic Egypt did.

At first priests added the leap day every third year by mistake, which Augustus corrected. The month Quintilis was renamed July for Caesar, and Sextilis became August.

The Julian year is about eleven minutes too long, so over centuries it drifted. The Gregorian calendar of 1582 fixed this. Russia kept the Julian calendar until 1918, and some Orthodox churches still use it for their feasts.
sum: The calendar of 365 days, with an extra day every fourth year, that Julius Caesar brought in from 1 January 45 BCE.
